newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FORECAST-NZ jobs data seen pivotal to any easing.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-NZ jobs data seen pivotal to any easing.

text.p: Slackening job and wages growth data expected in coming weeks should provide key evidence for a long-awaited monetary policy easing in New Zealand, economists said on Tuesday.
The Reserve Bank (RBNZ) has been wrestling with annual inflation on or outside the upper limit of its 0-2 percent target band for six quarters.

And despite lower-than-expected underlying inflation in the September year -- 2.34 percent against a forecast 2.7 percent -- the bank said it wanted further definitive evidence of lower inflation from other emerging indicators.
That should come principally via lower job growth data on Friday and wage growth figures due later in the month, according to 10 economists polled by Reuters.
This time last year the RB was dangling the prospect of an easing in front of people but over-exuberant markets jumped the gun and a more robust than expected economy saw the bank withdraw the lolly.
Economists are more confident now.

"We'd still say there should be an official easing in the December MPS (Monetary Policy Statement), taking conditions from tight to neutral...they (the RBNZ) might put some qualifications around it, but I don't think they're justified in delaying an official easing," said Bancorp executive director Roger Kerr.
"There is this expectation that the time is right for monetary conditions to start easing off," said Westpac Bank Economist Hamish Macalister.
The RBNZ may be looking to money supply and private sector credit data to complete the inflationary picture, Macalister said.
Economists forecast Friday's jobs data will show 0.2 percent employment growth in the September quarter, following surprisingly strong 0.9 percent June quarter growth.
Recent figures have shown the number of registered unemployed growing, while job ads have fallen from their highs.
Salary and wage rates are forecast to rise 1.9 percent in the September year, in data due on November 22.

The RB remains fearful of lower retail interest rates rekindling higher house prices which have been behind much of the inflation pressure over the past two years. That was one reason why it moved quickly last month to halt a debt market rally after the September quarter inflation data.
It warned then that the number in itself was not the evidence it needed that inflationary pressures were falling.
However, a week later, the bank appeared to acknowledge that it was over-doing things when it said in another statement that conditions had become overly tight.

Bankers Trust economist David Plank said while an official easing seemed likely in the December 17 MPS, it would be tempered by caution, as potential still existed for a fiscal blow-out following the country's inconclusive general election on October 12.

"We don't seem to be any closer to a resolution on who the next government is going to be...The probability of the RB going into the MPS not knowing the shape of the next government is increasing all the time."

The election left nationalist New Zealand First with the balance of power between the ruling conservative National Party and the main opposition Labour party, which promises more social spending. Coalition talks are seen taking several more weeks.
Plank said the RBNZ was acutely aware it might need to reassess its entire inflation outlook for 1997 if fiscal policy were loosened after the MPS.
"There are all sorts of problems, which may mean they hold on for a bit longer than people think, until that uncertainty is resolved," he said.
